body:
## What this guide helps you do

Choose the outcome, identify available assets and select the public Create or consultation path; do not expect a self-service site builder.

**Acceptance test:** Follow the public journey with a synthetic brief and verify all next steps are clear.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Define the brief and scope of delivery

A useful brief describes a business outcome, not just a preferred design. Start by identifying the intended audience, the problem they face and the action the site should make easier. A restaurant may need reliable booking enquiries; a portfolio may need visitors to understand a designer's work; a product platform may need authenticated account workflows. These are different projects even when their homepages look similar. Write the goal in one sentence and define how the team will evaluate it.

List the routes required for the first release. For each route, record its audience, main action, content owner, information dependencies and any integrations. Separate essential launch requirements from enhancements that can wait. A useful page inventory names actual pages, rather than a vague promise of an unlimited website. A feature inventory should describe behavior: for example, a booking request includes validation, receipt, scheduling rules and a human confirmation process. It is not just a button.

Prepare brand artwork, existing URLs, text, media, authorized account access and references. Never send passwords or service keys in a public brief. Mark each missing asset and assign responsibility for obtaining it. Determine whether existing content is ready, needs editing or must be created from scratch. For external references, specify what you like about the structure, not a demand to reproduce protected branding.

A scope review should agree deliverables, exclusions, revision checkpoints, payment milestones, dependencies, target dates and the person authorized to approve changes. Record unknowns as decisions to resolve during discovery. Changes after approval require an impact assessment rather than silent expansion of the project. A request is not an accepted contract; use [Create a project](/create/) or [Book a consultation](/book/) to begin the discussion.

## Prepare and review the guided project brief

The existing Project Creator is a guided intake workflow, not a public editor that automatically publishes sites. Its documented stages are Discover, Business, Design, Features, Scope, Investment and Send. Begin by selecting the project category that best describes the real business, then describe the intended audience, current challenges and desired outcome. If the project combines multiple categories, choose the primary one and describe the others in the brief rather than assuming the calculator can price every custom dependency.

During design selection, choose a visual direction and supply authorized references. The V5 design workspace demonstrates editing a separate concept; it does not modify the upstream repository or purchase a license. State how much motion the experience needs and which pages should remain untouched. During Features and Scope, select concrete functionality and count the core pages. Identify existing domain, hosting, backend, database, content, assets and required provider accounts. Separate payment or authentication integrations from simple static content because they require technical review.

Review Investment as a planning range. A budget preference expresses how much the visitor intends to spend; it is not a promise that every requested feature fits within that figure. If the displayed range exceeds the budget, reduce scope or ask the Studio about alternatives. Check the live brief for missing selections or contradictions before moving to Send.

In the standalone preview, export the draft for review. No form in that local demo creates a real enquiry, sends mail or issues an invitation. In an approved production implementation, wait for the server's acknowledgement before displaying success and retain the non-secret reference. If submission fails, keep the draft and retry only when appropriate. See [experience and navigation](/docs/experience/) and [pricing rules](/docs/pricing/).

## Navigation, information architecture and findability

Organize navigation by the tasks people actually perform. The Studio's public routes serve different goals: selected work establishes creative direction, design library supports discovery, pricing and Create support project planning, documentation answers questions, and the client portal supports authorized collaboration. A user should not need to understand internal implementation names to find those destinations. Use a small number of clear top-level links and a searchable directory for the deeper routes.

Give every page a meaningful title and a stable address. Use anchors for navigation and buttons for actions such as opening menus, changing filters or submitting a form. In a single-file preview, hash routes keep the demonstration local; real production pages should retain their existing canonical paths. A breadcrumb should show where an article sits within the library, and the current page should be distinguishable visually and semantically. Preserve back and forward navigation, direct entry and the ability to copy a useful article address.

For mobile navigation, ensure menus do not cover critical controls after dismissal. A modal menu needs predictable focus management, Escape handling and a way to restore focus to its trigger. Search should match meaningful titles, summaries, categories and common user terminology. A no-result state should suggest trying another phrase or using a relevant support route, rather than returning unrelated content. Do not make keyboard shortcuts the only way to open search.

Test navigation by task: find the price guidance, start a draft, find invitation help, read a policy and return to the previous page. Check keyboard-only operation, long category names, narrow screens, direct deep links and invalid paths. Keep the human [site map](/sitemap/) separate from the XML sitemap intended for crawlers. See [documentation](/docs/) and [Help Centre](/help/studio/).

## Triage, evidence collection and human handoff

Start support with a clear description of what the user was trying to accomplish. Ask for the affected public route, expected result, actual result, browser or device, approximate time and whether the problem repeats. Do not ask for passwords, invitation codes, payment card details or a complete private client record. A screenshot should be redacted before sharing. If the issue involves access, a non-secret project reference may help the team locate the request through its authorized systems.

Classify the symptom before choosing a fix. If navigation is unresponsive, check whether a menu or overlay is blocking input. If a creator step does not advance, inspect required fields and validation. If a pricing value looks incorrect, compare selected category, pages, features and configured allowances. If media fails, distinguish upload, storage authorization and playback. If a request appears lost, separate the server's acknowledgement from email delivery. If the issue affects a private account or security, escalate to the authorized team rather than attempting to bypass access restrictions.

Build a minimal reproduction with synthetic data wherever possible. Change one variable at a time and record whether the issue persists. Do not repeatedly submit a real enquiry, change DNS records or delete project data simply to diagnose a problem. For widespread issues, check the actual provider's official status information and approved Studio communication; do not invent an outage or resolution time.

A useful handoff includes symptom, impact, environment, reproducible steps, safe evidence, prior troubleshooting and requested outcome. The support assistant should link relevant guidance and admit uncertainty. Use [Report a bug](/report-bug/), [Contact the Studio](/contact/) or [Support AI](/support/), depending on the situation. The local preview can prepare a draft conversation but cannot file a real ticket or promise a response time.

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

Select the business category, describe audience and objective, shortlist a visual direction, choose features, review scope and investment, then prepare the brief.

## Sample brief for a small business

For a fictional local fitness studio, define the primary goal as qualified trial-session enquiries. Choose Business, list Home, Classes, About, Contact and FAQ, and note that the booking workflow requires a team confirmation rather than a guaranteed automated appointment. Provide an approved logo and existing service descriptions; mark missing imagery and legal copy as pending. Choose a visual reference based on readability and calls to action, not another brand's identity. Review the five-page scope and required features against the estimate, then export the brief. The exported record should include the audience, goal, selected pages, timeline preference, budget and outstanding decisions. The Studio team can use it to prepare a written proposal. No actual project is created when this sample is exported from the local preview.

## Interpret estimates, commercial decisions and worked examples

The repository planning model uses a category base and allowances to illustrate likely scope. The defaults inspected in planner-model.js include Business and Portfolio at ₹17,999, Ecommerce at ₹49,999, Agency at ₹29,999 and SaaS / platform at ₹199,999. These are source defaults, not guaranteed live CMS prices. A base includes up to four pages; the default allowance for each additional page is ₹1,500. Feature allowances vary, with a general default of ₹2,500 and named exceptions such as SEO foundations at ₹1,500, search and filters at ₹2,000 and API integrations at ₹3,500. The source supports configuration overrides.

For example, a business project with six pages, SEO foundations and search and filters has a lower planning estimate of ₹17,999 + ₹3,000 + ₹1,500 + ₹2,000 = ₹24,499. Under the default 25 percent contingency, with no additional technical-review features selected, the rounded upper estimate is ₹31,000. The upper range increases further for technical-review items; the actual model caps the additional percentage and rounds to the next ₹500. Do not apply the simple example to a bespoke platform without checking current configuration.

A written proposal should confirm what is included, what is optional, when fees become due, which provider costs are separate and who owns the accounts. Hosting, subscriptions, external licenses, taxes and ongoing maintenance may be additional. A template adaptation price covers the Studio's proposed work, not automatic transfer of upstream intellectual property. Review promotions for eligibility, dates, exclusions and actual published values. Never fabricate a discount, invoice or payment status. Use [Pricing](/pricing/) and [Project Creator](/create/) for planning, then request a written commercial review before accepting any charge.

## Form design, validation and submission behavior

A form should ask for the smallest set of information that supports its purpose. For a project enquiry, a name, reliable contact method and useful scope description may be sufficient to start. Group related fields and mark required inputs explicitly. Give each input a persistent, programmatically associated label and use the appropriate input type and autocomplete hint. Do not rely on a placeholder as the only label. For a long wizard, make the current step and progress clear while permitting users to review earlier answers without losing their draft.

Validate basic format and missing fields in the browser for immediate feedback, then validate all submitted values again on the server. Browser validation can be bypassed. Define permitted lengths, types and allowed values; reject unexpected or unauthorized properties. When an error occurs, associate the message with the relevant field, preserve valid input and move attention to a useful location without unnecessarily resetting the page. Avoid exposing internal exception details to visitors.

A submission has distinct states: editing, validation, request in progress, acknowledgement, failure and possibly a downstream notification. Do not display a success reference until the server confirms it. Email delivery is a separate operation from accepting an enquiry. In a local preview, clearly label export and demonstration actions; do not invent reference numbers that imply actual backend acceptance.

Test empty fields, invalid email, long text, repeated clicks, offline behavior, interrupted requests, keyboard use and mobile layout. Check that errors are readable and that no sensitive field appears in analytics or logs. For guidance, see the [W3C forms tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/) and [form instructions](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/instructions/).

title: Understand the editor
task: Distinguish preview canvas, editable concept inspector and production source; use the V5 design workspace for supported changes only.
check: Change a heading and viewport in a local concept, verify output, reset and confirm the source was not modified.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Distinguish preview canvas, editable concept inspector and production source; use the V5 design workspace for supported changes only.

**Acceptance test:** Change a heading and viewport in a local concept, verify output, reset and confirm the source was not modified.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## What the preview can and cannot edit

Choose an editable original concept in the design library and open its workspace. Change the brand name to a fictional example, modify the headline, and switch from desktop to phone. Inspect whether the headline wraps without clipping and whether the main action remains reachable. Change spacing and typography, then use Undo or Reset as supported by the visible controls. Export the HTML and inspect it in a separate browser tab. The preview is deliberately limited: it does not provide the full page-tree, drag-and-drop, account publishing or collaborative editing described in proposed product references. If a desired control is absent, document the requested capability and contact the Studio instead of attempting to edit the live application. The original third-party source URL is a separate reference and remains unchanged.

## Draft editing, preview controls and safe export

The V5 design workspace demonstrates a limited set of original concept editing controls: desktop, tablet and mobile viewport selection, editable brand and headline text, description, colors, typography, spacing, layout, motion preference, history, reset and export. These are local preview capabilities. The separate concept is not the third-party source website, and editing it does not modify the upstream project or create a published site. Full visual editor capabilities described in older handbook topics are implementation references unless separately verified in production.

Start by choosing a design direction that fits the intended content and audience. Inspect its source and licensing information before committing to a reference. Open the concept preview, select a viewport, and change one property at a time so its effect is clear. Try a realistic business name and heading, not only the default sample text. Review the placement of the main call to action and ensure the design still works when the copy is longer than expected. Compare desktop and phone views before selecting a direction.

Keep draft state separate from approved source and production configuration. An undo operation should restore the previous intended value; a reset should restore documented defaults, and destructive actions should have an appropriate warning. Export should reflect the visible current state and include sufficient metadata for the team to reproduce it. Open exported HTML separately and verify content and layout. If a future editor supports more advanced operations, define selection, nesting, drag alternatives, undo scope, autosave acknowledgement and conflict handling before advertising those capabilities.

Do not put private client records or credentials into example pages or exported drafts. See [design library](/design/), [preview and customization guide](/docs/field-notes/design-preview/) and [project creator](/create/) to transfer an approved direction into a project brief.

## Responsive layout, content flow and device adaptation

Start with the content order and primary action, then define a flexible layout. Use semantic HTML and normal document flow so the page remains useful even if animation or decorative assets fail. A desktop editorial grid may place supporting copy beside a main article, while a narrow screen should move that supporting material below or into an accessible disclosure. Avoid fixing every element to the dimensions of a design screenshot. Content length, zoom, translations and browser defaults change the actual space available.

Use CSS Grid for two-dimensional relationships and Flexbox for aligned sequences. For example, a responsive card container can use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr)) to avoid a minimum card width exceeding a small viewport. Grid and flex children often need min-width: 0 so long text can wrap instead of expanding the container. Set media to max-width: 100% and provide suitable dimensions. Use overflow-wrap for long URLs or identifiers. Horizontal scrolling is appropriate for genuinely wide data tables, not the entire document.

Choose breakpoints when the content stops fitting, not simply according to specific phone names. Test 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels as representative widths, plus intermediate widths and browser zoom. Check header, footer, dialogs, sticky navigation, form errors and unusually long titles. A responsive preview canvas is an inspection aid; it does not replace real devices or assistive technology.

When diagnosing overflow, inspect the first element extending beyond its containing block and review computed width, min-width, positioning, whitespace and transforms. Fix the underlying cause rather than hiding the overflow and losing access to content. Review [MDN responsive design](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/CSS_layout/Responsive_Design) and [CSS Grid](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/CSS_layout/Grids).

## Verification matrix, test evidence and acceptance

A useful quality plan starts with the tasks the intended users need to complete, then adds failure paths and risk-based checks. For each test, record the route, version, environment, device or viewport, preconditions, input, expected result, actual result and evidence. Distinguish a browser emulation from a physical device and distinguish a local prototype from the configured staging or live website. Do not mark an untested integration as passed because its interface rendered correctly.

Begin with representative journeys: browse work, search the design library, open a reference, adjust an editable concept, create a project brief, read pricing, find a documentation article, ask for help and attempt authorized client access. Check back and forward navigation, direct route entry, keyboard focus, long content, loading states, no-result states and invalid links. For forms, test missing fields, duplicate input and network failure. For private workflows, use synthetic accounts and verify both allowed and denied operations.

Use a device matrix that reflects actual customers. Representative widths such as 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels help reveal layout problems, but include intermediate widths, zoom and real touch interaction. Check accessibility, motion preferences, image failures and performance on lower-powered hardware. Automated checks can detect regressions in expected DOM structure, links and state transitions; manual checks are still needed for readability, assistive technology and quality of interaction.

Classify findings by impact and urgency. An issue that leaks private data or prevents a core task should block release. A cosmetic issue may be deferred only with an accountable owner and documented decision. Reproduce the original defect after its fix and inspect related behavior. See [QA and release gates](/docs/quality/), [W3C accessibility guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [web performance](https://web.dev/performance).

## Accessibility acceptance and interaction semantics

Accessibility must be assessed through actual use, not only a design screenshot or a successful automated scan. Start with semantic landmarks, meaningful headings and native controls. A link should navigate; a button should perform an action. Inputs need persistent labels, and icons used as controls need accessible names. Make the focus order match the logical task order. Use visible focus indicators that are not hidden by sticky headers or overlays, and do not remove the browser's focus outline without providing a suitable replacement.

Check contrast against WCAG 2.2: normal text generally needs at least 4.5:1 contrast and large text at least 3:1 under the applicable AA criteria. For meaningful visual boundaries and state indicators, evaluate the relevant non-text contrast requirement. Avoid conveying error, selection or approval using color alone. Check text zoom and reflow, including a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport where applicable. Provide a readable alternative for information in images, and captions or suitable alternatives for meaningful audiovisual content.

Test all essential actions using only the keyboard. Open and close dialogs, navigate menus, submit forms and recover from errors. Modal dialogs should keep focus in the intended interaction and return it appropriately on dismissal. For touch, avoid crowding controls; WCAG 2.2 includes a 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target size criterion with exceptions, and larger targets can improve usability. Respect reduced-motion preferences; do not require movement to reveal essential content. Provide a pause or equivalent control for applicable moving content.

Record actual findings and retest fixes. Automated scanners are helpful but cannot prove full conformance. Consult [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag/), [W3C understanding documents](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [accessibility tutorials](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/).

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

If an exact time, price or limit depends on live configuration, link to that source and avoid inventing a value.

For errors, state what happened, whether the user's information was saved, and the safest next action. A useful message might say that the request could not be confirmed and the draft is still available, rather than reporting success or exposing a stack trace. Use persistent labels, short paragraphs, descriptive links and meaningful headings. Avoid ambiguous links such as repeated Click here, particularly in documentation and emails.

Review public copy with realistic content and on narrow screens. Check whether a reader unfamiliar with Studio terminology can follow the procedure. Link claims to current policies, pricing, documentation or verified provider references. Record the version of commercial or legal content that was approved, and route unresolved claims to the responsible team. See [website terms](/terms/) and [support](/support/).

Start with the content order and primary action, then define a flexible layout. Use semantic HTML and normal document flow so the page remains useful even if animation or decorative assets fail. A desktop editorial grid may place supporting copy beside a main article, while a narrow screen should move that supporting material below or into an accessible disclosure. Avoid fixing every element to the dimensions of a design screenshot. Content length, zoom, translations and browser defaults change the actual space available.

Use CSS Grid for two-dimensional relationships and Flexbox for aligned sequences. For example, a responsive card container can use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr)) to avoid a minimum card width exceeding a small viewport. When diagnosing overflow, inspect the first element extending beyond its containing block and review computed width, min-width, positioning, whitespace and transforms. Fix the underlying cause rather than hiding the overflow and losing access to content. ## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

title: Make a site responsive
task: Test actual content at 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels; identify overflow, wrapping, clipping and inaccessible sticky controls.
check: Check navigation, forms, media and reading order on real touch and keyboard devices.

## What this guide helps you do

Test actual content at 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels; identify overflow, wrapping, clipping and inaccessible sticky controls.

**Acceptance test:** Check navigation, forms, media and reading order on real touch and keyboard devices.

Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Responsive test example

Open a content-heavy article and a pricing form at 320 and 390 CSS pixels. Verify that the article text remains readable, headings wrap and the on-page contents disclosure is usable. On the pricing form, test a long feature label, a validation message and the result panel. Rotate a real phone or change the emulated width to an intermediate size, then inspect the desktop layout at 1440. If the body scrolls horizontally, locate the widest element using the browser inspector and review its width constraints; do not mask the symptom by clipping the whole document. Repeat with browser zoom and reduced motion enabled. Record each issue with its route, width, observed result and intended fix. title: Use AI to build a site
task: Prepare a brief with scope, required content and protected elements; treat AI output as a reviewable proposal, not a published website.
check: Review generated copy for false claims, inspect dependencies and approve only an explicit draft change.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Prepare a brief with scope, required content and protected elements; treat AI output as a reviewable proposal, not a published website.

**Acceptance test:** Review generated copy for false claims, inspect dependencies and approve only an explicit draft change.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## AI assistance, retrieval, evaluation and limits

Public support AI should answer from a defined knowledge collection, not from access to all Studio systems. Start by identifying the assistant's purpose and permitted actions. Help AI can locate public articles, Project AI can explain the brief and estimates, and private project assistance requires a separate authorization boundary. The V5 preview uses local guidance retrieval; it does not make a Gemini API request or access private client records. A production integration requires configured server credentials, current provider settings and verified request handlers.

For retrieval, index only approved public material with stable article IDs, titles, sections, revision metadata and source links. Rank passages against the question, supply the model with the relevant excerpts and require it to distinguish verified facts from suggestions. If evidence is weak, ask for clarification or offer a support route rather than fabricating a policy, price or capability. Do not treat a model-generated citation as verified merely because it resembles a URL; resolve citations against the actual indexed documents.

Treat both user input and retrieved text as untrusted data. Instructions embedded in an article, attachment or website must not override application rules. Authorization and allowed tool actions belong outside the model. Restrict tools to the minimum necessary and require an explicit user decision before sending or changing consequential information. Public assistants should never retrieve private client files based on a guessed reference. Avoid exposing prompts, keys or sensitive conversation details in error messages.

Evaluate with known-answer questions, ambiguous requests, unsupported features, pricing, multilingual variations, privacy requests and prompt-injection attempts. Score accuracy, source relevance, abstention and useful escalation independently. Keep a deterministic help fallback if the model is unavailable. See [project AI](/docs/project-ai/), [support sources](/docs/field-notes/support-sources/) and [OWASP prompt injection prevention](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

## Prepare and review the guided project brief

The existing Project Creator is a guided intake workflow, not a public editor that automatically publishes sites. Its documented stages are Discover, Business, Design, Features, Scope, Investment and Send. Begin by selecting the project category that best describes the real business, then describe the intended audience, current challenges and desired outcome. If the project combines multiple categories, choose the primary one and describe the others in the brief rather than assuming the calculator can price every custom dependency.

During design selection, choose a visual direction and supply authorized references. The V5 design workspace demonstrates editing a separate concept; it does not modify the upstream repository or purchase a license. State how much motion the experience needs and which pages should remain untouched. During Features and Scope, select concrete functionality and count the core pages. Identify existing domain, hosting, backend, database, content, assets and required provider accounts. Separate payment or authentication integrations from simple static content because they require technical review.

Review Investment as a planning range. A budget preference expresses how much the visitor intends to spend; it is not a promise that every requested feature fits within that figure. If the displayed range exceeds the budget, reduce scope or ask the Studio about alternatives. Check the live brief for missing selections or contradictions before moving to Send.

In the standalone preview, export the draft for review. No form in that local demo creates a real enquiry, sends mail or issues an invitation. In an approved production implementation, wait for the server's acknowledgement before displaying success and retain the non-secret reference. If submission fails, keep the draft and retry only when appropriate. See [experience and navigation](/docs/experience/) and [pricing rules](/docs/pricing/).

## Draft editing, preview controls and safe export

The V5 design workspace demonstrates a limited set of original concept editing controls: desktop, tablet and mobile viewport selection, editable brand and headline text, description, colors, typography, spacing, layout, motion preference, history, reset and export. These are local preview capabilities. The separate concept is not the third-party source website, and editing it does not modify the upstream project or create a published site. Full visual editor capabilities described in older handbook topics are implementation references unless separately verified in production.

Start by choosing a design direction that fits the intended content and audience. Inspect its source and licensing information before committing to a reference. Open the concept preview, select a viewport, and change one property at a time so its effect is clear. Try a realistic business name and heading, not only the default sample text. Review the placement of the main call to action and ensure the design still works when the copy is longer than expected. Compare desktop and phone views before selecting a direction.

Keep draft state separate from approved source and production configuration. An undo operation should restore the previous intended value; a reset should restore documented defaults, and destructive actions should have an appropriate warning. Export should reflect the visible current state and include sufficient metadata for the team to reproduce it. Open exported HTML separately and verify content and layout. If a future editor supports more advanced operations, define selection, nesting, drag alternatives, undo scope, autosave acknowledgement and conflict handling before advertising those capabilities.

Do not put private client records or credentials into example pages or exported drafts. See [design library](/design/), [preview and customization guide](/docs/field-notes/design-preview/) and [project creator](/create/) to transfer an approved direction into a project brief.

## Source provenance, copyright and licensing review

A visually impressive reference is not automatically reusable. A public GitHub repository may have a license that permits some uses, no clear license at all, or separate terms for bundled code, fonts, illustrations and photographs. Before adapting a design, record its exact source URL, author, version or commit, stated license, component dependencies and asset provenance. Keep the original license and copyright notices with the source package whenever required. Verify the license in the repository itself rather than relying solely on a catalogue label.

In the existing Veloryz catalogue, entries distinguish candidate, review-required and restricted sources. A candidate status does not prove that every asset may be sold or redistributed; restricted entries should not be offered as reusable templates. A project containing copyleft code may involve obligations that differ from a permissively licensed component. Consult the applicable license text and qualified legal advice when obligations are unclear. A screenshot or public live demo is evidence of appearance, not a grant of rights.

Create a rights register with a row for each major asset or dependency. Example fields: item, file path, source, author, version, license, permitted use, attribution, replacement requirement, reviewer and evidence date. Separate official Studio logos and original concept assets from upstream materials. Do not remove a third-party creator's credit where attribution is required. For generated or supplied imagery, confirm the permitted use and whether the output misleadingly depicts an actual client project.

The written project agreement should distinguish original deliverables, licensed dependencies, account ownership and any rights transferred at handover. The Studio's fee for customization or development does not mean the client acquires ownership of upstream code. See [copyright guide](/docs/copyright/), [design library](/design/) and [GitHub's licensing documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/licensing-a-repository).

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

Modal dialogs should keep focus in the intended interaction and return it appropriately on dismissal. For touch, avoid crowding controls; WCAG 2.2 includes a 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target size criterion with exceptions, and larger targets can improve usability. Respect reduced-motion preferences; do not require movement to reveal essential content. Provide a pause or equivalent control for applicable moving content.

Record actual findings and retest fixes. Automated scanners are helpful but cannot prove full conformance. Consult [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag/), [W3C understanding documents](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [accessibility tutorials](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/).

## Data minimization, consent and privacy-aware operation

Before collecting any data, write a short record of what information is needed, why it is collected, where it goes, who can access it and when it should be removed. A project brief may need a contact method and project details; a technical bug report may need a route and browser version. Neither normally requires passwords, full identity documents, payment card numbers or another client's information. Optional fields should be clearly optional and sensitive attachments should use the authorized private channel.

Distinguish browser storage used for essential session or consent functions from optional preferences and measurements. The repository's inspected privacy code describes essential storage, optional functional preferences, local-only measurement and inactive advertising tracking. Treat this as a source description to verify against the actual deployment; do not assume that every third-party embed or future feature follows the same policy. Document the live storage keys, expiration behavior, consent choices and provider relationships before publication. A visitor should be able to revise optional choices without losing access to essential content.

For AI workflows, send only the context needed to answer the public question. Avoid transferring confidential files or private records to a model merely because a conversation asks for them. Review provider contracts, data processing and retention settings with the responsible team. For access or deletion requests, use the Studio's published privacy channel and avoid requesting sensitive proof in the first message. Actual identity verification, exemptions and retention decisions depend on applicable law and agreed procedures.

Use the [privacy policy](/privacy/), [cookie policy](/cookies/) and [privacy choices](/privacy/choices/) for published notices. The technical guide is an implementation and review aid, not a legal compliance opinion. Review the actual data flow again whenever authentication, analytics, AI, payment or storage integrations change.

- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.

title: Preview and publish
task: Review preview content, links, forms and mobile behavior; obtain approval and deploy the exact reviewed revision using the configured host.
check: Verify the public URL, release identifier, status and recovery plan after deployment.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Review preview content, links, forms and mobile behavior; obtain approval and deploy the exact reviewed revision using the configured host.

**Acceptance test:** Verify the public URL, release identifier, status and recovery plan after deployment.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Publishing rehearsal without production changes

Take the approved local preview and identify the source revision that would be integrated. Create an isolated staging build with synthetic data and verify the route map, protected homepage and Services page, asset paths, documentation and form states. Confirm the hosting configuration and required server bindings without disclosing secrets. Ask the reviewer to approve the exact staged revision; capture the approval and test evidence. Before deploying, identify the previous working version and assess whether any database migration changes recovery. Once authorized, use the configured deployment workflow and test the actual public URL, not just the build log. If the deployment cannot be verified, report the release as unconfirmed. The current standalone preview is not a deployment candidate without integration and regression testing.

## Controlled publishing, environment separation and rollback

A local preview, a staging environment and a production website have different responsibilities. The preview allows visual and interaction review without committing or deploying. Staging should exercise the intended build against an isolated configuration and synthetic data. Production serves real visitors and may process actual project requests or private records. Do not connect an experimental preview to live write endpoints simply to make a demonstration feel functional. Use environment-specific credentials and clearly identify the environment in review records.

Prepare a release candidate with an immutable identifier, a list of changes and an explicit protected scope. In this project the approved homepage and Services page are protected unless separately authorized. Review route differences, assets, configuration, database changes and dependency updates. Confirm that the build is reproducible using the repository's package manager and scripts. Keep the last healthy deployment and understand whether new database migrations or data written by the new version would be compatible with a rollback. Code rollback does not automatically undo database changes.

Before publishing, run acceptance tests and obtain explicit approval. Verify production bindings, custom-domain routing, access rules and environment secrets through authorized tools. After a release, test the actual public URL and key paths: navigation, pricing, project creation, documentation, authentication and authorized resource access. Monitor errors and latency using the configured observability tools, without logging sensitive information. Record the release identifier, approval and outcome.

If a critical regression appears, stop further rollout, identify the affected version and choose the safest recovery path. Cloudflare documents [versions and deployments](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/versions-and-deployments/) and [rollbacks](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/versions-and-deployments/rollbacks/). Review provider limitations and data compatibility before using a rollback. See [release QA](/docs/quality/).

## Verification matrix, test evidence and acceptance

A useful quality plan starts with the tasks the intended users need to complete, then adds failure paths and risk-based checks. For each test, record the route, version, environment, device or viewport, preconditions, input, expected result, actual result and evidence. Distinguish a browser emulation from a physical device and distinguish a local prototype from the configured staging or live website. Do not mark an untested integration as passed because its interface rendered correctly.

Begin with representative journeys: browse work, search the design library, open a reference, adjust an editable concept, create a project brief, read pricing, find a documentation article, ask for help and attempt authorized client access. Check back and forward navigation, direct route entry, keyboard focus, long content, loading states, no-result states and invalid links. For forms, test missing fields, duplicate input and network failure. For private workflows, use synthetic accounts and verify both allowed and denied operations.

Use a device matrix that reflects actual customers. Representative widths such as 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels help reveal layout problems, but include intermediate widths, zoom and real touch interaction. Check accessibility, motion preferences, image failures and performance on lower-powered hardware. Automated checks can detect regressions in expected DOM structure, links and state transitions; manual checks are still needed for readability, assistive technology and quality of interaction.

Classify findings by impact and urgency. An issue that leaks private data or prevents a core task should block release. A cosmetic issue may be deferred only with an accountable owner and documented decision. Reproduce the original defect after its fix and inspect related behavior. See [QA and release gates](/docs/quality/), [W3C accessibility guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [web performance](https://web.dev/performance).

## Search visibility, canonical addresses and crawler-facing documents

Search engine optimization begins with useful public content and stable routes. Give each public page a descriptive title, meaningful main heading and content that helps the intended audience. A documentation article should answer a specific task and link naturally to related articles; do not create dozens of nearly identical pages solely to target keywords. Use semantic HTML and descriptive link labels so users and crawlers can understand the page structure. Provide appropriate image alternatives and readable content without requiring decorative animation.

Maintain a canonical address for each indexable page. Where the Studio has both trailing-slash and .html documentation addresses, decide which address is canonical in the actual deployment, preserve useful redirects or links and avoid conflicting signals. The standalone preview uses local hash routes for review; those are not production indexable article URLs. Keep previews and private account routes outside the public indexing strategy. Authentication is required to protect private content; a robots rule or noindex tag is not an access-control mechanism.

Generate the XML sitemap from the approved list of public canonical pages. Include only valid indexable URLs and accurate modification dates when available. Separately maintain a human-readable site map organized by task and topic. Check internal links, status codes, redirect chains, missing pages, canonical metadata and rendered HTML before submitting a sitemap through the authorized search console. A sitemap helps discovery but does not guarantee indexing or ranking.

Review indexing reports and search performance using the actual configured tools. Avoid interpreting a local preview as search visibility evidence. If a route is missing from search, distinguish crawlability, indexing and ranking before making changes. See [Google crawling and indexing](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing), [canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) and [sitemap creation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap).

## Performance measurement, rendering budgets and optimization

Performance must be measured against the user's actual task. A page can animate smoothly on a powerful desktop while responding slowly to taps or taking too long to display content on a phone. Use repeatable lab tests to investigate bottlenecks and field data when available to understand the experience of real visitors. Core Web Vitals distinguish loading, interaction responsiveness and visual stability. Good thresholds commonly used by web.dev are LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less and CLS of 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile; these are targets, not measurements of this website.

Start with the critical rendering path. Identify the main content element, reduce render-blocking resources, serve appropriately sized images and reserve layout space for media. Avoid lazy-loading the primary above-the-fold image if it is essential to the initial view. Use lazy loading for noncritical galleries and defer expensive optional features. Keep font loading and fallback choices from causing avoidable shifts. For a large design catalogue, render a bounded page of results rather than creating all heavy preview frames at once.

For responsiveness, profile representative actions: opening navigation, typing a search query, selecting a creator option, opening an article and interacting with the model. Look for long JavaScript tasks, unnecessary synchronous layout work and background animation loops. Reduce the amount of work per interaction and break expensive operations into suitable smaller tasks. Verify that changes preserve the intended experience and do not simply hide or disable a required feature.

Compare baseline and updated results under the same device, browser and network conditions. Record test method and observed metrics; never infer production field performance from a local screenshot. See [web.dev Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals), [optimize LCP](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp) and [optimize INP](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp).

- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

## Domain configuration, routing, certificates and redirects

A domain connection has several independent layers: registration, authoritative DNS, provider routing, TLS certificate issuance and application behavior. A domain that resolves is not necessarily routed to the right Worker, and a routed domain may still have a certificate or redirect problem.

Review existing records before editing them; unrelated email verification, mail delivery and other services may depend on records in the same zone. Make a targeted change only when the desired record and its impact are known. Do not remove unrelated DNS records during troubleshooting. Follow the provider's domain setup procedure, allowing for verification and certificate provisioning where needed. Never share account credentials or API tokens in public documentation.

Check that HTTPS presents a valid certificate for the requested hostname, then inspect HTTP responses and redirect destinations. A redirect loop, missing route and certificate mismatch require different fixes. Test both canonical and alternate hostnames, direct deep links and the expected HTTP-to-HTTPS behavior. Preserve working email and other subdomains.

Keep a record of the old configuration and recovery path before an approved change. Do not report a domain as ready until it is reachable and behaves correctly from a normal visitor's browser. ## What this guide helps you do

Distinguish private client membership from administrator access; invite only verified recipients and remove access when no longer required.

**Acceptance test:** Test one authorized and one unrelated account with synthetic records.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Authorization, roles and private resource boundaries

Authentication proves the identity of a caller; authorization determines what that identity may do. Define permissions against resources and actions, not just broad labels. For example, an authorized client may read files belonging to an assigned project but cannot read files of another project, change pricing configuration or manage Studio users. An anonymous visitor may read published CMS content but should not retrieve private enquiry records. An administrator's access must be verified through the actual server session, not a role string supplied by the browser.

Use a deny-by-default approach. At each protected request, check session validity, requested operation and resource ownership or membership. Keep privileged credentials on the server and do not put a service-role key in client JavaScript. When Supabase is used, design grants and Row Level Security policies for the relevant tables and storage objects. Test both reads and writes. A policy allowing a user to select a record does not necessarily authorize updating it. The same applies to download and upload permissions.

Build a negative test matrix with anonymous access, correct member, unrelated member, revoked member, expired session and administrator. Use synthetic records and check both the browser view and direct server responses. Verify that errors reveal neither private object existence nor confidential details beyond what the caller needs. Audit relevant role changes and access revocation using minimal metadata, with appropriate log access restrictions.

For an invitation workflow, verify expiration, intended recipient, assignment and single-use behavior when that is required by the implementation. Revoke access when collaboration ends. Do not document untested security as a guarantee. Review [OWASP authorization guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Supabase RLS](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) for implementation patterns.

## Client collaboration, invitations and project milestones

A project reference identifies a request or project. It must not act as a password or substitute for authorization. A client invitation is a separate credential issued through an approved process; treat it as confidential and do not send it through public support or AI. Verify the intended recipient, project assignment and expiration using the actual server-side workflow before access is granted. If an invitation is unavailable, contact the Studio with the non-secret project reference, not a guessed code or another person's record.

The proposed client workspace organizes collaboration around a small set of tasks: review the current milestone, inspect approved files, respond to a requested decision, view the next action and prepare handover. The V5 demonstration uses fictional sample data and local controls. It does not show actual projects, grant real access or transmit feedback. Production must load only records authorized for the authenticated user; a hidden tab or omitted menu is not an access control.

For each milestone, identify the deliverable, reviewer, approval criteria, planned window and dependencies. A status should reflect the actual project record: a draft is not approved, a review request is not a completion, and a completed milestone does not necessarily mean the project is paid or launched. Feedback should point to the specific version, screen or element and describe the expected result. Keep unresolved decisions visible until they are accepted or closed.

At handover, confirm which source files, media, configuration instructions, account ownership, notices and support arrangements are included in the written agreement. Review access removal and outstanding invoices separately from technical delivery. See [Client portal](/client/), [portal reference](/docs/client-portal/) and [process](/process/).

Before collecting any data, write a short record of what information is needed, why it is collected, where it goes, who can access it and when it should be removed. A project brief may need a contact method and project details; a technical bug report may need a route and browser version. Neither normally requires passwords, full identity documents, payment card numbers or another client's information. Optional fields should be clearly optional and sensitive attachments should use the authorized private channel.

Distinguish browser storage used for essential session or consent functions from optional preferences and measurements. The repository's inspected privacy code describes essential storage, optional functional preferences, local-only measurement and inactive advertising tracking. Treat this as a source description to verify against the actual deployment; do not assume that every third-party embed or future feature follows the same policy. A visitor should be able to revise optional choices without losing access to essential content.

For AI workflows, send only the context needed to answer the public question. Avoid transferring confidential files or private records to a model merely because a conversation asks for them. Review provider contracts, data processing and retention settings with the responsible team. For access or deletion requests, use the Studio's published privacy channel and avoid requesting sensitive proof in the first message. Actual identity verification, exemptions and retention decisions depend on applicable law and agreed procedures.

Use the [privacy policy](/privacy/), [cookie policy](/cookies/) and [privacy choices](/privacy/choices/) for published notices. The technical guide is an implementation and review aid, not a legal compliance opinion. ## Versioned collaboration, review and handover

A project review is a decision about an identifiable version, not an informal collection of comments across unrelated channels. At the beginning of the project, assign responsibility for providing content, reviewing design, approving commercial changes and accepting delivery. Identify who can make decisions on behalf of the client and who operates the Studio's deployment. Keep access limited to the people and resources required for those responsibilities.

When requesting feedback, name the version or preview, affected page or component and the decision needed. Useful feedback describes the problem, expected result and priority. For example, a mobile creator button that is covered by a sticky panel is actionable; a request to make everything better should be clarified into review criteria. Record whether each comment is open, addressed or accepted. Do not resolve a review item simply because a developer marked the change complete; confirm the result with the appropriate reviewer.

Do not silently overwrite a newer approved version. A version record should identify the author, timestamp, scope and change reason. Before restoring a prior version, determine which newer changes would be lost and whether database or configuration differences matter. In the local V5 preview, feedback and edits are only demonstrations; do not assume they were submitted to the Studio.

Prepare the handover with agreed source files, licensed assets and notices, configuration instructions, ownership details, test evidence and known limitations. title: Billing and plans
task: Read the written agreement and itemized estimate; separate third-party provider fees, taxes and maintenance from implementation costs.
check: Reconcile the approved proposal and invoice without sending card information in chat.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Read the written agreement and itemized estimate; separate third-party provider fees, taxes and maintenance from implementation costs.

**Acceptance test:** Reconcile the approved proposal and invoice without sending card information in chat.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Interpret estimates, commercial decisions and worked examples

The repository planning model uses a category base and allowances to illustrate likely scope. The defaults inspected in planner-model.js include Business and Portfolio at ₹17,999, Ecommerce at ₹49,999, Agency at ₹29,999 and SaaS / platform at ₹199,999. These are source defaults, not guaranteed live CMS prices. A base includes up to four pages; the default allowance for each additional page is ₹1,500. Feature allowances vary, with a general default of ₹2,500 and named exceptions such as SEO foundations at ₹1,500, search and filters at ₹2,000 and API integrations at ₹3,500. The source supports configuration overrides.

For example, a business project with six pages, SEO foundations and search and filters has a lower planning estimate of ₹17,999 + ₹3,000 + ₹1,500 + ₹2,000 = ₹24,499. Under the default 25 percent contingency, with no additional technical-review features selected, the rounded upper estimate is ₹31,000. The upper range increases further for technical-review items; the actual model caps the additional percentage and rounds to the next ₹500. Do not apply the simple example to a bespoke platform without checking current configuration.

A written proposal should confirm what is included, what is optional, when fees become due, which provider costs are separate and who owns the accounts. Hosting, subscriptions, external licenses, taxes and ongoing maintenance may be additional. A template adaptation price covers the Studio's proposed work, not automatic transfer of upstream intellectual property. Review promotions for eligibility, dates, exclusions and actual published values. Never fabricate a discount, invoice or payment status. Use [Pricing](/pricing/) and [Project Creator](/create/) for planning, then request a written commercial review before accepting any charge.

## Define the brief and scope of delivery

A useful brief describes a business outcome, not just a preferred design. Start by identifying the intended audience, the problem they face and the action the site should make easier. A restaurant may need reliable booking enquiries; a portfolio may need visitors to understand a designer's work; a product platform may need authenticated account workflows. These are different projects even when their homepages look similar. Write the goal in one sentence and define how the team will evaluate it.

List the routes required for the first release. For each route, record its audience, main action, content owner, information dependencies and any integrations. Separate essential launch requirements from enhancements that can wait. A useful page inventory names actual pages, rather than a vague promise of an unlimited website. A feature inventory should describe behavior: for example, a booking request includes validation, receipt, scheduling rules and a human confirmation process. It is not just a button.

Prepare brand artwork, existing URLs, text, media, authorized account access and references. Never send passwords or service keys in a public brief. Mark each missing asset and assign responsibility for obtaining it. Determine whether existing content is ready, needs editing or must be created from scratch. For external references, specify what you like about the structure, not a demand to reproduce protected branding.

A scope review should agree deliverables, exclusions, revision checkpoints, payment milestones, dependencies, target dates and the person authorized to approve changes. Record unknowns as decisions to resolve during discovery. Changes after approval require an impact assessment rather than silent expansion of the project. A request is not an accepted contract; use [Create a project](/create/) or [Book a consultation](/book/) to begin the discussion.

## Write accurate, accessible and actionable content

Use language that helps a reader decide what to do next. Start with a clear title describing the task, explain prerequisites and make the main action unambiguous. Avoid broad claims such as guaranteed delivery, unlimited features, complete security or instant publication unless they are supported by a written agreement and verified implementation. Distinguish an estimate from an approved quote, a booking request from a confirmed meeting, a draft from a published version, and a local demonstration from a functioning production service.

Use the Studio's team-based voice rather than personal ownership claims on public pages. When writing help content, use the same names for controls that appear in the interface. For example, a guide to the design preview should say Desktop, Tablet, Mobile, Export and Reset only when those controls are present in the reviewed version. If a capability is still a proposal, identify it as such and describe what the user can do today instead. If an exact time, price or limit depends on live configuration, link to that source and avoid inventing a value.

For errors, state what happened, whether the user's information was saved, and the safest next action. A useful message might say that the request could not be confirmed and the draft is still available, rather than reporting success or exposing a stack trace. Use persistent labels, short paragraphs, descriptive links and meaningful headings. Avoid ambiguous links such as repeated Click here, particularly in documentation and emails.

Review public copy with realistic content and on narrow screens. Check whether a reader unfamiliar with Studio terminology can follow the procedure. **Acceptance test:** Record whether the request is accepted, deferred or rejected without implying a release date.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Versioned collaboration, review and handover

A project review is a decision about an identifiable version, not an informal collection of comments across unrelated channels. At the beginning of the project, assign responsibility for providing content, reviewing design, approving commercial changes and accepting delivery. Identify who can make decisions on behalf of the client and who operates the Studio's deployment. Keep access limited to the people and resources required for those responsibilities.

When requesting feedback, name the version or preview, affected page or component and the decision needed. Useful feedback describes the problem, expected result and priority. For example, a mobile creator button that is covered by a sticky panel is actionable; a request to make everything better should be clarified into review criteria. Record whether each comment is open, addressed or accepted. Do not resolve a review item simply because a developer marked the change complete; confirm the result with the appropriate reviewer.

Maintain a clear distinction between local draft, approved revision and deployed release. If multiple people may edit the same content, define how conflicts are detected and resolved. Do not silently overwrite a newer approved version. A version record should identify the author, timestamp, scope and change reason. Before restoring a prior version, determine which newer changes would be lost and whether database or configuration differences matter. In the local V5 preview, feedback and edits are only demonstrations; do not assume they were submitted to the Studio.

Prepare the handover with agreed source files, licensed assets and notices, configuration instructions, ownership details, test evidence and known limitations. Keep actual secret values out of exported instructions. ## Define the brief and scope of delivery

A useful brief describes a business outcome, not just a preferred design. Start by identifying the intended audience, the problem they face and the action the site should make easier. A restaurant may need reliable booking enquiries; a portfolio may need visitors to understand a designer's work; a product platform may need authenticated account workflows. These are different projects even when their homepages look similar. Write the goal in one sentence and define how the team will evaluate it.

List the routes required for the first release. For each route, record its audience, main action, content owner, information dependencies and any integrations. Separate essential launch requirements from enhancements that can wait. A useful page inventory names actual pages, rather than a vague promise of an unlimited website. A feature inventory should describe behavior: for example, a booking request includes validation, receipt, scheduling rules and a human confirmation process. It is not just a button.

Prepare brand artwork, existing URLs, text, media, authorized account access and references. Never send passwords or service keys in a public brief. Mark each missing asset and assign responsibility for obtaining it. Determine whether existing content is ready, needs editing or must be created from scratch. For external references, specify what you like about the structure, not a demand to reproduce protected branding.

A scope review should agree deliverables, exclusions, revision checkpoints, payment milestones, dependencies, target dates and the person authorized to approve changes. Record unknowns as decisions to resolve during discovery. Changes after approval require an impact assessment rather than silent expansion of the project. A request is not an accepted contract; use [Create a project](/create/) or [Book a consultation](/book/) to begin the discussion.

## Triage, evidence collection and human handoff

Start support with a clear description of what the user was trying to accomplish. Ask for the affected public route, expected result, actual result, browser or device, approximate time and whether the problem repeats. Do not ask for passwords, invitation codes, payment card details or a complete private client record. A screenshot should be redacted before sharing. If the issue involves access, a non-secret project reference may help the team locate the request through its authorized systems.

Classify the symptom before choosing a fix. If navigation is unresponsive, check whether a menu or overlay is blocking input. If a creator step does not advance, inspect required fields and validation. If a pricing value looks incorrect, compare selected category, pages, features and configured allowances. If media fails, distinguish upload, storage authorization and playback. If a request appears lost, separate the server's acknowledgement from email delivery. If the issue affects a private account or security, escalate to the authorized team rather than attempting to bypass access restrictions.

Build a minimal reproduction with synthetic data wherever possible. Change one variable at a time and record whether the issue persists. Do not repeatedly submit a real enquiry, change DNS records or delete project data simply to diagnose a problem. For widespread issues, check the actual provider's official status information and approved Studio communication; do not invent an outage or resolution time.

A useful handoff includes symptom, impact, environment, reproducible steps, safe evidence, prior troubleshooting and requested outcome. The support assistant should link relevant guidance and admit uncertainty. Use [Report a bug](/report-bug/), [Contact the Studio](/contact/) or [Support AI](/support/), depending on the situation. The local preview can prepare a draft conversation but cannot file a real ticket or promise a response time.

## Write accurate, accessible and actionable content

Use language that helps a reader decide what to do next. Start with a clear title describing the task, explain prerequisites and make the main action unambiguous. Avoid broad claims such as guaranteed delivery, unlimited features, complete security or instant publication unless they are supported by a written agreement and verified implementation. Distinguish an estimate from an approved quote, a booking request from a confirmed meeting, a draft from a published version, and a local demonstration from a functioning production service.

Use the Studio's team-based voice rather than personal ownership claims on public pages. When writing help content, use the same names for controls that appear in the interface. For example, a guide to the design preview should say Desktop, Tablet, Mobile, Export and Reset only when those controls are present in the reviewed version. If a capability is still a proposal, identify it as such and describe what the user can do today instead. If an exact time, price or limit depends on live configuration, link to that source and avoid inventing a value.

For errors, state what happened, whether the user's information was saved, and the safest next action. A useful message might say that the request could not be confirmed and the draft is still available, rather than reporting success or exposing a stack trace. Use persistent labels, short paragraphs, descriptive links and meaningful headings. Avoid ambiguous links such as repeated Click here, particularly in documentation and emails.

Review public copy with realistic content and on narrow screens. Check whether a reader unfamiliar with Studio terminology can follow the procedure. Link claims to current policies, pricing, documentation or verified provider references. Record the version of commercial or legal content that was approved, and route unresolved claims to the responsible team. See [website terms](/terms/) and [support](/support/).

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.
