title: AI integration and evaluation plan
task: Design public retrieval, model fallback, role isolation and evaluation; validate citations and consequential actions outside the model.
check: Test multilingual prompts, weak matches, malicious instructions and private-record requests.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Design public retrieval, model fallback, role isolation and evaluation; validate citations and consequential actions outside the model.

**Acceptance test:** Test multilingual prompts, weak matches, malicious instructions and private-record requests.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Original field-guide notes

**Ground responses in approved content.** Use a server-side retrieval layer restricted to public, approved articles and current CMS facts. Provide source IDs, abstain on weak matches and distinguish suggestions from contractual terms.

**Guard the execution boundary.** Treat prompts and retrieved articles as untrusted text. Restrict tools and data access by authenticated role; keep keys in server configuration and require confirmation before consequential actions.

**Evaluate before launch.** Use test questions for pricing, ambiguity, unsupported requests, multilingual queries and private-record access. Measure answer relevance, citation accuracy, safe refusal and human handoff.

## Model evaluation checklist example

Create a small benchmark with known public answers, ambiguous requests, out-of-scope account requests and attempts to override the assistant using instructions embedded in a fictional article. Test Hindi and English queries where the intended product supports both. For each question, specify the approved source, expected answer boundaries and whether a human handoff is necessary. Measure citation validity and accuracy separately from tone. Test provider timeout and verify a deterministic fallback that links to relevant public guides. For any proposed tool action, enforce authorization and confirmation in the application rather than trusting the model's decision. Keep private project records outside the public retrieval index. Review failures before enabling the live Gemini integration. Do not claim the benchmark passed unless the actual configured service was tested; local scripted responses only demonstrate the UI and basic retrieval behavior.

## AI assistance, retrieval, evaluation and limits

Public support AI should answer from a defined knowledge collection, not from access to all Studio systems. Start by identifying the assistant's purpose and permitted actions. Help AI can locate public articles, Project AI can explain the brief and estimates, and private project assistance requires a separate authorization boundary. The V5 preview uses local guidance retrieval; it does not make a Gemini API request or access private client records. A production integration requires configured server credentials, current provider settings and verified request handlers.

For retrieval, index only approved public material with stable article IDs, titles, sections, revision metadata and source links. Rank passages against the question, supply the model with the relevant excerpts and require it to distinguish verified facts from suggestions. If evidence is weak, ask for clarification or offer a support route rather than fabricating a policy, price or capability. Do not treat a model-generated citation as verified merely because it resembles a URL; resolve citations against the actual indexed documents.

Treat both user input and retrieved text as untrusted data. Instructions embedded in an article, attachment or website must not override application rules. Authorization and allowed tool actions belong outside the model. Restrict tools to the minimum necessary and require an explicit user decision before sending or changing consequential information. Public assistants should never retrieve private client files based on a guessed reference. Avoid exposing prompts, keys or sensitive conversation details in error messages.

Evaluate with known-answer questions, ambiguous requests, unsupported features, pricing, multilingual variations, privacy requests and prompt-injection attempts. Score accuracy, source relevance, abstention and useful escalation independently. Keep a deterministic help fallback if the model is unavailable. See [project AI](/docs/project-ai/), [support sources](/docs/field-notes/support-sources/) and [OWASP prompt injection prevention](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

## Integration contracts, validation and failure recovery

An integration connects two distinct systems. Begin with a contract that identifies the caller, operation, required inputs, response schema, authentication, authorization and error behavior. In the inspected repository, the public project flows refer to POST /api/enquiries, POST /api/project-ai and GET /api/site, alongside private client-portal routes. Confirm the deployed handlers before publishing any detailed endpoint contract. The presence of a route name does not prove a particular request schema, rate limit or production configuration. Keep private API details out of public examples unless they have been approved for publication.

For a write operation, validate the input on the server and reject fields that are not part of the intended operation. Use a request identifier or another reviewed idempotency design for operations that must not be duplicated. Separate the primary database transaction from downstream effects such as sending email. If an enquiry is accepted but an email fails, the system should distinguish those outcomes and support a safe recovery procedure. Do not blindly retry a write after an ambiguous network failure; first establish whether the operation was accepted.

Credentials belong in the server environment or an approved secret-management mechanism. The browser should receive only the minimal public configuration it requires. Validate authorization for protected operations independently of the interface. For external callbacks or webhooks, verify authenticity and replay controls according to the provider's current documented protocol before processing the payload. Use timeouts and bounded retries for transient failures; avoid exposing raw provider exceptions to customers.

Test valid, invalid, missing, duplicated and unauthorized requests with synthetic data. Record expected response, actual behavior and a correlation identifier that does not reveal private details. See [technical architecture](/docs/architecture/) and [Supabase API security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api).

## Security review, safe defaults and incident boundaries

Begin with the resources that need protection: project enquiries, private milestones, client files, administrative configuration, API credentials and any sensitive logs. Identify the public entry points, trusted server boundaries, database and storage permissions, and external services. Use this map to determine how a visitor could attempt to access or modify an unauthorized resource. The aim is to prevent a class of failure rather than hide the corresponding button in the interface.

Validate untrusted input at each server boundary and safely render user-controlled content. Keep credentials and privileged keys outside client JavaScript, public documentation and downloadable briefs. Enforce authentication and authorization on every protected request. When a file is uploaded, review permitted types, size, storage location and access policy. When a model or third-party embed is used, constrain its access and treat content as untrusted. Avoid returning raw stack traces, sensitive configuration or private data in errors. Apply appropriate rate controls to exposed actions, with actual limits defined and reviewed by the responsible team.

Use synthetic test records to verify access denial, invalid data handling, expired sessions, revoked membership and duplicate requests. Review dependency versions and the deployment environment before release. Record each finding with impact, affected boundary, evidence, mitigation, owner and retest. Security testing should be performed only on authorized systems and avoid disrupting real customers. Do not claim that the site is completely secure or certified because a local interface was tested.

If an incident is suspected, protect affected access, retain appropriate evidence and contact the authorized team. Share only the necessary details through a suitable private channel. The approved privacy and incident procedures determine further response and notification. Review [OWASP Cheat Sheets](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/), [Supabase product security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security) and [security guide](/security/).

## Documentation structure, evidence and editorial governance

A useful knowledge base should distinguish task guides, reference documentation, troubleshooting and policy material. A task guide leads the reader through a real outcome; a technical reference explains parameters, boundaries and examples; a troubleshooting guide starts with a symptom and helps isolate the cause; a policy describes approved commitments. Do not combine these into one vague article that repeats the product slogan. Assign each article a stable route and a clearly described audience.

For each article, record the source version, its availability status, related routes and the team responsible for review. Explain whether the information describes a verified public control, a reviewed source implementation or a proposed operating procedure. If the current preview does not expose a capability, make that clear early in the article and provide an alternative path. Link to the actual source documentation and current published policies rather than silently rewriting legal commitments. Use external primary sources, such as official standards or provider documentation, for technical details; cite them where they are useful, not merely as a long undifferentiated bibliography.

Build the article with headings, a short outcome statement, prerequisites, steps, a realistic example, failure handling and acceptance criteria. Link related concepts inline and use a topic-specific table of contents. Long guides should be navigable and printable; the article directory should support search and category filters. Do not count navigation labels, related-link titles or repeated boilerplate as substantive article length. Shared technical sections should be identified so authors can maintain them once and reviewers can recognize overlap.

Before publishing a documentation change, check internal links, external reference addresses, headings, accessible link labels, article metadata and factual claims. Keep canonical routes unchanged unless an approved redirect is provided. For a release, review the article diff and source version with the responsible team. See [GitHub review guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/review-pull-requests/reviewing-proposed-changes-in-a-pull-request) and [Studio documentation](/docs/studio/).

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Start with the task described at the beginning of this article and identify the responsible reviewer.
- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

title: Review responsive design before approval
task: Test realistic content on desktop, tablet and mobile; examine touch, keyboard, wrapping and interaction speed.
check: Record browser, viewport, content case and result for every issue.
body:
## What this guide helps you do

Test realistic content on desktop, tablet and mobile; examine touch, keyboard, wrapping and interaction speed.

**Acceptance test:** Record browser, viewport, content case and result for every issue.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Original field-guide notes

**Test content, not just a screenshot.** Check every important task on desktop, tablet and phone. Use long titles, translated copy, validation errors and realistic content lengths.

**Review interactions.** Confirm touch targets, keyboard focus, scroll containment and screen reader labels. Test a slower device and verify menus and sticky panels do not cover content.

**Record and resolve exceptions.** Capture the viewport and exact issue. Approve only after the layout and essential tasks work across the supported browser matrix.

## Responsive layout, content flow and device adaptation

Start with the content order and primary action, then define a flexible layout. Use semantic HTML and normal document flow so the page remains useful even if animation or decorative assets fail. A desktop editorial grid may place supporting copy beside a main article, while a narrow screen should move that supporting material below or into an accessible disclosure. Avoid fixing every element to the dimensions of a design screenshot. Content length, zoom, translations and browser defaults change the actual space available.

Use CSS Grid for two-dimensional relationships and Flexbox for aligned sequences. For example, a responsive card container can use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr)) to avoid a minimum card width exceeding a small viewport. Grid and flex children often need min-width: 0 so long text can wrap instead of expanding the container. Set media to max-width: 100% and provide suitable dimensions. Use overflow-wrap for long URLs or identifiers. Horizontal scrolling is appropriate for genuinely wide data tables, not the entire document.

Choose breakpoints when the content stops fitting, not simply according to specific phone names. Test 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels as representative widths, plus intermediate widths and browser zoom. Check header, footer, dialogs, sticky navigation, form errors and unusually long titles. A responsive preview canvas is an inspection aid; it does not replace real devices or assistive technology.

When diagnosing overflow, inspect the first element extending beyond its containing block and review computed width, min-width, positioning, whitespace and transforms. Fix the underlying cause rather than hiding the overflow and losing access to content. Review [MDN responsive design](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/CSS_layout/Responsive_Design) and [CSS Grid](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/CSS_layout/Grids).

## Accessibility acceptance and interaction semantics

Accessibility must be assessed through actual use, not only a design screenshot or a successful automated scan. Start with semantic landmarks, meaningful headings and native controls. A link should navigate; a button should perform an action. Inputs need persistent labels, and icons used as controls need accessible names. Make the focus order match the logical task order. Use visible focus indicators that are not hidden by sticky headers or overlays, and do not remove the browser's focus outline without providing a suitable replacement.

Check contrast against WCAG 2.2: normal text generally needs at least 4.5:1 contrast and large text at least 3:1 under the applicable AA criteria. For meaningful visual boundaries and state indicators, evaluate the relevant non-text contrast requirement. Avoid conveying error, selection or approval using color alone. Check text zoom and reflow, including a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport where applicable. Provide a readable alternative for information in images, and captions or suitable alternatives for meaningful audiovisual content.

Test all essential actions using only the keyboard. Open and close dialogs, navigate menus, submit forms and recover from errors. Modal dialogs should keep focus in the intended interaction and return it appropriately on dismissal. For touch, avoid crowding controls; WCAG 2.2 includes a 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target size criterion with exceptions, and larger targets can improve usability. Respect reduced-motion preferences; do not require movement to reveal essential content. Provide a pause or equivalent control for applicable moving content.

Record actual findings and retest fixes. Automated scanners are helpful but cannot prove full conformance. Consult [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag/), [W3C understanding documents](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [accessibility tutorials](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/).

## Verification matrix, test evidence and acceptance

A useful quality plan starts with the tasks the intended users need to complete, then adds failure paths and risk-based checks. For each test, record the route, version, environment, device or viewport, preconditions, input, expected result, actual result and evidence. Distinguish a browser emulation from a physical device and distinguish a local prototype from the configured staging or live website. Do not mark an untested integration as passed because its interface rendered correctly.

Begin with representative journeys: browse work, search the design library, open a reference, adjust an editable concept, create a project brief, read pricing, find a documentation article, ask for help and attempt authorized client access. Check back and forward navigation, direct route entry, keyboard focus, long content, loading states, no-result states and invalid links. For forms, test missing fields, duplicate input and network failure. For private workflows, use synthetic accounts and verify both allowed and denied operations.

Use a device matrix that reflects actual customers. Representative widths such as 320, 390, 768 and 1440 CSS pixels help reveal layout problems, but include intermediate widths, zoom and real touch interaction. Check accessibility, motion preferences, image failures and performance on lower-powered hardware. Automated checks can detect regressions in expected DOM structure, links and state transitions; manual checks are still needed for readability, assistive technology and quality of interaction.

Classify findings by impact and urgency. An issue that leaks private data or prevents a core task should block release. A cosmetic issue may be deferred only with an accountable owner and documented decision. Reproduce the original defect after its fix and inspect related behavior. See [QA and release gates](/docs/quality/), [W3C accessibility guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/) and [web performance](https://web.dev/performance).

## Performance measurement, rendering budgets and optimization

Performance must be measured against the user's actual task. A page can animate smoothly on a powerful desktop while responding slowly to taps or taking too long to display content on a phone. Use repeatable lab tests to investigate bottlenecks and field data when available to understand the experience of real visitors. Core Web Vitals distinguish loading, interaction responsiveness and visual stability. Good thresholds commonly used by web.dev are LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less and CLS of 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile; these are targets, not measurements of this website.

Start with the critical rendering path. Identify the main content element, reduce render-blocking resources, serve appropriately sized images and reserve layout space for media. Avoid lazy-loading the primary above-the-fold image if it is essential to the initial view. Use lazy loading for noncritical galleries and defer expensive optional features. Keep font loading and fallback choices from causing avoidable shifts. For a large design catalogue, render a bounded page of results rather than creating all heavy preview frames at once.

For responsiveness, profile representative actions: opening navigation, typing a search query, selecting a creator option, opening an article and interacting with the model. Look for long JavaScript tasks, unnecessary synchronous layout work and background animation loops. Reduce the amount of work per interaction and break expensive operations into suitable smaller tasks. Verify that changes preserve the intended experience and do not simply hide or disable a required feature.

Compare baseline and updated results under the same device, browser and network conditions. Record test method and observed metrics; never infer production field performance from a local screenshot. See [web.dev Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals), [optimize LCP](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp) and [optimize INP](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp).

## Apply the guidance and record the result

- Verify the article-specific acceptance test above.
- Record the tested revision, observed result, remaining limitations and any decision requiring team approval.

## What this guide helps you do

Collect the minimum project information, distinguish optional storage and route rights requests to the team.

**Acceptance test:** Confirm no private records enter public AI, screenshots or exported demo briefs.

This is an editorial review edition for VELORYZ Studio. It distinguishes the standalone preview, documented repository behavior and proposed production work. Only operate controls and records that are actually available to your authorized role. The technical sections below are selected shared handbook modules; they provide the broader implementation and review context for this specific task.

## Original field-guide notes

**Collect only what is necessary.** Ask for the project goal, contact method and essential scope. Avoid sensitive details in public AI, demo forms and shared screenshots.

**Review optional preferences.** Distinguish necessary session storage from optional preferences and analytics. Allow a reversible choice and document the actual storage and providers.

**Handle requests securely.** Use the published privacy contact for access or deletion requests. Do not claim compliance or a retention guarantee until actual data flows and legal obligations have been reviewed.

## Data minimization, consent and privacy-aware operation

Before collecting any data, write a short record of what information is needed, why it is collected, where it goes, who can access it and when it should be removed. A project brief may need a contact method and project details; a technical bug report may need a route and browser version. Neither normally requires passwords, full identity documents, payment card numbers or another client's information. Optional fields should be clearly optional and sensitive attachments should use the authorized private channel.

Distinguish browser storage used for essential session or consent functions from optional preferences and measurements. The repository's inspected privacy code describes essential storage, optional functional preferences, local-only measurement and inactive advertising tracking. Treat this as a source description to verify against the actual deployment; do not assume that every third-party embed or future feature follows the same policy. Document the live storage keys, expiration behavior, consent choices and provider relationships before publication. A visitor should be able to revise optional choices without losing access to essential content.

For AI workflows, send only the context needed to answer the public question. Avoid transferring confidential files or private records to a model merely because a conversation asks for them. Review provider contracts, data processing and retention settings with the responsible team. For access or deletion requests, use the Studio's published privacy channel and avoid requesting sensitive proof in the first message. Actual identity verification, exemptions and retention decisions depend on applicable law and agreed procedures.

Use the [privacy policy](/privacy/), [cookie policy](/cookies/) and [privacy choices](/privacy/choices/) for published notices. The technical guide is an implementation and review aid, not a legal compliance opinion. Review the actual data flow again whenever authentication, analytics, AI, payment or storage integrations change.

## Authorization, roles and private resource boundaries

Authentication proves the identity of a caller; authorization determines what that identity may do. Define permissions against resources and actions, not just broad labels. For example, an authorized client may read files belonging to an assigned project but cannot read files of another project, change pricing configuration or manage Studio users. An anonymous visitor may read published CMS content but should not retrieve private enquiry records. An administrator's access must be verified through the actual server session, not a role string supplied by the browser.

Use a deny-by-default approach. At each protected request, check session validity, requested operation and resource ownership or membership. Keep privileged credentials on the server and do not put a service-role key in client JavaScript. When Supabase is used, design grants and Row Level Security policies for the relevant tables and storage objects. Test both reads and writes. A policy allowing a user to select a record does not necessarily authorize updating it. The same applies to download and upload permissions.

Build a negative test matrix with anonymous access, correct member, unrelated member, revoked member, expired session and administrator. Use synthetic records and check both the browser view and direct server responses. Verify that errors reveal neither private object existence nor confidential details beyond what the caller needs. Audit relevant role changes and access revocation using minimal metadata, with appropriate log access restrictions.

For an invitation workflow, verify expiration, intended recipient, assignment and single-use behavior when that is required by the implementation. Revoke access when collaboration ends. Do not document untested security as a guarantee. Review [OWASP authorization guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Supabase RLS](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) for implementation patterns.

## Client collaboration, invitations and project milestones

A project reference identifies a request or project. It must not act as a password or substitute for authorization. A client invitation is a separate credential issued through an approved process; treat it as confidential and do not send it through public support or AI. Verify the intended recipient, project assignment and expiration using the actual server-side workflow before access is granted. If an invitation is unavailable, contact the Studio with the non-secret project reference, not a guessed code or another person's record.

The proposed client workspace organizes collaboration around a small set of tasks: review the current milestone, inspect approved files, respond to a requested decision, view the next action and prepare handover. The V5 demonstration uses fictional sample data and local controls. It does not show actual projects, grant real access or transmit feedback. Production must load only records authorized for the authenticated user; a hidden tab or omitted menu is not an access control.

For each milestone, identify the deliverable, reviewer, approval criteria, planned window and dependencies. A status should reflect the actual project record: a draft is not approved, a review request is not a completion, and a completed milestone does not necessarily mean the project is paid or launched. Feedback should point to the specific version, screen or element and describe the expected result. Keep unresolved decisions visible until they are accepted or closed.

At handover, confirm which source files, media, configuration instructions, account ownership, notices and support arrangements are included in the written agreement. Review access removal and outstanding invoices separately from technical delivery. See [Client portal](/client/), [portal reference](/docs/client-portal/) and [process](/process/).

## Security review, safe defaults and incident boundaries

Begin with the resources that need protection: project enquiries, private milestones, client files, administrative configuration, API credentials and any sensitive logs. Identify the public entry points, trusted server boundaries, database and storage permissions, and external services. Use this map to determine how a visitor could attempt to access or modify an unauthorized resource. The aim is to prevent a class of failure rather than hide the corresponding button in the interface.

Validate untrusted input at each server boundary and safely render user-controlled content. Keep credentials and privileged keys outside client JavaScript, public documentation and downloadable briefs. Enforce authentication and authorization on every protected request. When a file is uploaded, review permitted types, size, storage location and access policy. When a model or third-party embed is used, constrain its access and treat content as untrusted. Avoid returning raw stack traces, sensitive configuration or private data in errors. Apply appropriate rate controls to exposed actions, with actual limits defined and reviewed by the responsible team.

Use synthetic test records to verify access denial, invalid data handling, expired sessions, revoked membership and duplicate requests. Review dependency versions and the deployment environment before release. Record each finding with impact, affected boundary, evidence, mitigation, owner and retest. Security testing should be performed only on authorized systems and avoid disrupting real customers. Do not claim that the site is completely secure or certified because a local interface was tested.

If an incident is suspected, protect affected access, retain appropriate evidence and contact the authorized team. Share only the necessary details through a suitable private channel. The approved privacy and incident procedures determine further response and notification. Review [OWASP Cheat Sheets](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/), [Supabase product security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/product-security) and [security guide](/security/).

title: Handling a privacy request from receipt to resolution
task: Prepare a privacy request without exposing sensitive information, and understand the studio’s review process.
check: Verify identity proportionately, record the decision, and explain the result through an authorised channel.
body:
## Start with the right request

A privacy request concerns personal information, not necessarily a project deliverable or an ordinary service complaint. A visitor may want to know what information the studio holds, correct inaccurate contact details, ask for erasure, withdraw an optional preference or raise a grievance. Begin by identifying which outcome is required. Use the [privacy request preparation page](/privacy/request/) to draft a message, or contact the studio through the address in the published [privacy policy](/privacy/). The preparation form does not submit a server request. The email client opens only when the visitor chooses that action. Avoid creating another account simply to ask about your information.

## What to include and what to leave out

State the request type, a short description of the information concerned and, when useful, the non-secret project reference. An existing email correspondence may help the studio identify the relevant relationship. Do not provide payment card numbers, login passwords, private invitation tokens, government identity documents or an entire confidential project file in the first message. If additional identification is necessary, the team should explain why and establish an appropriate protected verification method. A public assistant cannot authenticate a requester or exercise rights on behalf of the requester. For a billing dispute rather than a privacy request, use the [contact page](/contact/) and refer to the agreed project terms.

## Intake and acknowledgment

For the studio team, open an internal request record with a unique reference, receipt time, requested action, responsible reviewer and communication channel. Keep this record separate from a public support transcript. The team should acknowledge receipt through an appropriate channel and explain the next step. Do not promise a fixed legal deadline without checking which legal framework applies and whether a particular clock starts at receipt, verification or another relevant event. Escalate suspected breaches through the [security page](/security/) rather than treating an active exposure as a routine data correction.

## Verify the requester proportionately

Compare the request with the relationship already established in the client or enquiry system. A message from a familiar email address may support a low-risk correction, but changing access permissions or exporting personal records requires stronger verification. Do not rely on the public project reference alone: it is not an authentication credential. If the request is made by a representative, establish their authority before releasing information. Document the verification decision without storing unnecessary identity evidence. Where the team cannot establish the necessary authority, explain what is missing rather than silently releasing records or rejecting the request without a reason.

## Locate the information

Use the approved record inventory to identify the relevant enquiry, correspondence, client workspace, file metadata and any provider-managed records. The public repository describes enquiry and client workflows and identifies possible service providers, but the actual deployed provider inventory must be confirmed. A record held in a service provider's infrastructure may have separate access and deletion controls. Restrict retrieval to the requester's authorised records. In particular, do not use an unrestricted service-role database credential in a browser or give a public AI assistant access to another customer's data. Record which systems were checked, who checked them and which systems could not be verified.

## Evaluate the requested action

For access, prepare a scoped account of the information that may be disclosed, with redaction for unrelated individuals or confidential third-party information where appropriate. For correction, update the authoritative record and identify downstream copies that need to remain consistent. For erasure, determine whether the record can be removed or must be retained for an applicable legal, contractual, accounting or dispute-related reason. Withdrawal of optional consent should stop the relevant optional processing where applicable; it does not automatically invalidate all prior lawful processing or terminate an agreed project. When obligations conflict, obtain qualified advice rather than relying on a generic policy statement.

## Verify completion and communicate the outcome

After a permitted change, verify the authoritative record and the expected user-facing result. A successful API response is not enough if stale copies or downstream systems continue to expose the old value. Record any remaining backup retention or delayed provider action accurately. Tell the requester what was done, what could not be done, the reason for any limitation and how to raise a follow-up concern. Deliver any sensitive export using an authorised channel, not a public link or an open chat transcript. Keep only the minimum internal evidence required to demonstrate responsible handling.

## Worked example: an outdated project email

Imagine a client asks to replace the email address attached to a project. First establish whether this is simply a contact correction or a transfer of authenticated account access. If it changes access, verify the requester through the existing trusted relationship and confirm who should own the workspace. Update only the intended record, check that a previous invitation cannot accidentally grant the wrong person access, and confirm delivery of any new invitation without exposing its secret. Do not send the entire project archive to an unverified replacement address. The team should record the correction and separately confirm the new communication route.

## Worked example: clearing browser choices

A visitor may ask to delete all information after clearing cookies. Explain that clearing local storage affects that browser and does not itself erase enquiry messages or client records held by a server. Direct the visitor to [privacy choices](/privacy/choices/) for local controls and to the request preparation page for server-side questions. In the preview, rejecting optional preferences does not transmit anything to production. In the deployed application, verify that optional processing is stopped and that any permitted consent receipt is handled according to the approved policy.

## Release and escalation checklist

Before publishing a privacy request process, confirm the responsible legal entity, contact details, grievance escalation path, applicable response requirements, record-class retention schedule, provider obligations and identity-verification procedure. Test that a visitor can locate the process on a mobile device, navigate without an account, reject optional processing and contact the studio without exposing credentials. Test a correction against a non-production record, including authorised and unauthorised cases, and retain a redacted audit trail. The team should review unresolved cases periodically and ensure that changes to privacy law or infrastructure trigger a documented policy review. India’s DPDP framework is phased; consult the official notification and current legal advice before stating specific statutory rights or dates. This playbook is a proposed operational procedure based on the repository and published sources, not evidence that a complete rights-request workflow has already been deployed.

title: Verify cookies, storage and consent before release
task: Distinguish essential browser state from optional preferences and verify actual storage behaviour before publishing a notice.
check: Record a clean-browser inventory, verify reject and withdrawal paths, and reconcile actual provider activity.
body:
## Begin with evidence, not a banner design

A cookie notice should describe what the application actually stores and why. A consent banner is only one part of that responsibility. Start from the application source, then inspect the deployed browser and the server configuration. The Veloryz repository includes a privacy controller and a local-only quality measurement module. The code describes a consent-choice key, optional measurement keys, preference cleanup and a best-effort consent receipt request. This establishes the intended implementation, not the contents of a real production browser session. The [cookie policy](/cookies/) identifies this distinction explicitly. Do not publish a claim that the application uses no trackers simply because one module contains no tracker script.

## Understand the storage mechanisms

HTTP cookies can be sent automatically with matching requests and may be used for an authenticated session. Their attributes determine when they are sent, whether JavaScript can access them and when they expire. Local storage is normally persistent for an origin until cleared; session storage is scoped to a browsing context. Application code decides how long a stored value remains valid. Browser expiry, eviction and private-browsing behaviour can vary. A preference key and a session authentication cookie have different purposes, even when both are stored on the same device. A notice should therefore address cookies and comparable browser technologies rather than treating every value as a cookie.

## Create the inventory

In a clean browser profile, open the site without signing in. Inspect cookies, local storage, session storage and network requests before accepting optional processing. For each item, record its name, origin, purpose, category, trigger, expected expiry or retention rule, recipient if any, and whether it remains after rejecting optional categories. Identify whether the evidence came from a source file, a browser observation or a provider contract. Record uncertainty when a server-controlled cookie is not visible to JavaScript. Review embedded fonts, videos, images, payment frames and analytics separately: a third-party request is not necessarily a tracker, but it may disclose request metadata. Repeat after an application update because the inventory can change.

## Inspect the repository controls

The inspected privacy controller names `veloryz.privacy.choice.v1` as its consent-selection key, uses a version and timestamp, and rejects choices older than approximately 180 days. It defines `veloryz.measurement.optin.v1` and `veloryz.measurement.local.v1` for optional measurement. Its cleanup paths address dismissed consultation and invitation prompts and keys beginning with `vz-campaign:`. It checks Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals when determining optional measurement. The controller also contains a receipt identifier and a best-effort request to `/api/privacy/consent`. Check those code paths against the version actually deployed. The presence of a receipt call does not prove that the database stores a receipt or that any particular server retention policy is active.

## Test the decision paths independently

Use a separate clean session for each test. First reject optional storage and navigate several public pages. Check whether optional keys or unexpected network destinations appear. Then test accepting optional preferences only, accepting optional measurement where available, and accepting all available optional categories. Confirm that a disabled advertising category is not silently enabled. Reopen settings and withdraw the choices. Verify that optional values and associated processing are removed or disabled as intended. Reload and navigate again to make sure the new decision persists. When a global privacy signal is present, check that optional measurement is disabled according to the implemented rule. Check both desktop and mobile layouts and keyboard navigation.

## Keep required functions usable

Declining optional processing should not prevent a visitor from reading documentation, accessing public pricing information or making an enquiry where required processing is separately explained. Authentication state for a private portal is not the same as optional marketing state. If clearing site data ends an authenticated session, explain that as an expected effect rather than suggesting all cookies are unnecessary. Test whether essential protections remain active in reject mode. A visitor must also be able to find privacy information without being blocked by a consent dialog. The settings entry should remain accessible after the initial choice, and reject and accept actions should be comparably clear.

## Worked example: inconsistent measurement state

Suppose a test browser initially accepts optional measurement, then changes the choice to reject. The UI reports success, but the optional measurement counter still exists. Check whether the cleanup routine ran, whether another script re-created the key, whether the browser's saved consent state was stale and whether the published bundle matches the inspected source. Stop optional measurement until the inconsistency is understood. A screenshot of the banner alone cannot establish that processing stopped. Retest by navigating and reloading after withdrawal. Record the final browser observation and source revision, without collecting real customer browsing history.

## Worked example: adding a third-party embed

A new project preview embeds an external video. Before release, identify the network requests initiated before playback, cookies or storage set by the embed, whether the user can choose when to load it, and the external provider's privacy information. If the embed introduces optional processing, determine which choice category applies and ensure the relevant mechanism respects it. Consider a static preview with a deliberate external link when that provides the same benefit with fewer unexpected disclosures. Update the inventory and notice; do not label an embed essential solely because the visual design uses it.

## Publish only after reconciliation

The person responsible for publication should compare the inventory against the public notice, confirm actual session cookie flags and lifetimes, check provider configuration and review record retention. The production policy should distinguish the live application from a downloadable preview, whose local bookmarks and example preferences may use different storage keys. The [Trust Centre](/trust/) identifies unresolved items instead of hiding them behind a compliance label. Review the legal basis and applicable consent requirements with qualified counsel, especially when services or user groups change. Retain a versioned inventory, a redacted test record, the approved wording and a review date. If an unexpected script or optional request appears after release, disable or isolate it while the team investigates and update the notice only after confirming the facts. A real policy is an ongoing operational commitment, not an attractive static page.

title: Resolve a support issue with a clear handoff
task: Identify the affected workflow, follow a safe first check, and prepare an actionable support summary.
check: Provide a reproducible, redacted report and select the correct public or authorised support route.
body:
## Choose the right support route

Start with the outcome you need, rather than the name of the interface. If you are considering a project, read the [pricing guide](/docs/pricing/) or open [Create](/create/). If you already have an approved project and need access, use the [client portal guidance](/docs/client-portal/). For a broken page or interaction, use [Report a bug](/report-bug/) after recording the behaviour. Privacy requests have their own [preparation page](/privacy/request/). A public support conversation is useful for finding information but cannot verify an account, approve a commercial exception, inspect private files or confirm a production deployment. The local assistant in this preview retrieves guides and prepares a handoff; it does not call a live model or send a support ticket.

## Write the issue in one sentence

Describe the action, expected result and observed result. For example, “On the project creator Features step, selecting a checkbox changes the estimate but the Continue button stays disabled.” That is more actionable than “the website does not work.” Include the public URL, browser, device type, approximate time and the shortest steps that reproduce the issue. If the problem is intermittent, record whether it occurs after navigation, after a particular selection or only on one device. Distinguish a complete failure from a cosmetic inconsistency. This allows the team to choose the appropriate area and assess the impact without requiring the visitor to repeat the entire story.

## Perform safe first checks

Reload the affected page once, check the network connection and verify required fields. For an enquiry submission, do not repeatedly press submit if a request may already have reached the server. Keep any displayed public reference. For an issue limited to a specific browser, compare behaviour in a different browser or clean browsing session if possible. Do not clear all browser data before saving a local draft or considering whether you might lose a signed-in session. Do not disable security controls or change DNS records simply because an automated assistant suggests it. A first check should be reversible, proportionate and appropriate to the affected workflow.

## Protect private information in evidence

A screenshot often helps, but crop or redact email addresses, names, payment details, private project content, access codes and tokens. Do not send browser storage dumps or a full network archive if they may include session credentials. A team member investigating an authenticated workflow should use a dedicated authorised test account and synthetic records. Public URLs, a non-secret reference and an error identifier may be sufficient for the initial report. If more evidence is required, the team should explain the requested material, who will access it and which secure channel to use. A support issue does not justify collecting unrelated personal data.

## Identify the impact and escalation path

A typographical error or inconsistent spacing usually requires an editorial or visual correction. An inaccessible navigation control, a form that cannot submit or a broken client invitation may block a key task and should be escalated accordingly. Suspected unauthorized access, exposed secrets or another person's private records require the security reporting path rather than ordinary public troubleshooting. If the user is asking about a billing or contractual commitment, route the case to the responsible team member; do not treat a generic AI response as an approved commercial decision. The studio should communicate any confirmed incident or operational limitation using verified information rather than an assumed status.

## What a useful local answer looks like

The assistant should identify the question, use relevant documentation, explain one or two safe actions and link to the precise supporting pages. When the answer depends on live account status, a configuration setting or an unpublished policy, state that limitation and offer the correct human handoff. It should not claim to have created a ticket, checked a database or spoken to a human unless the corresponding action was actually completed. If the visitor supplies an ambiguous description, ask for the affected page or outcome rather than guessing. For a sensitive request, warn against sharing credentials and offer the appropriate protected route. Consult the [support sources guide](/docs/field-notes/support-sources/) for the knowledge boundary.

## Worked example: an invitation is missing

A client says that a project reference is accepted but the invitation email did not arrive. Explain that these are different values. Ask whether the studio has approved portal access and whether the email address used for correspondence is correct. The client can check spam or filtering, but should not post an activation token into the public chat. If the invitation is still missing, the team must confirm the relevant record and delivery status through its authorised tools. If an invitation has expired, the team should follow the approved regeneration and revocation procedure. The local preview cannot inspect the actual mailbox or invitation database. Link the client portal guide and contact page rather than promising that a replacement was issued.

## Worked example: a design preview fails to load

Determine whether the failure affects the local editable concept, a remote image, or an upstream live demo. A remote demo may be unavailable, block framing or require a separate network connection. Open the original source link if safe, and distinguish a source outage from a bug in the Veloryz preview workspace. Do not silently substitute an unrelated template and describe it as the original. Capture the affected design identifier and the visible error. If the design's licence or assets are unresolved, route that issue to licensing review rather than treating it as a missing image. The [design library](/design/) and [copyright page](/copyright/) explain these boundaries.

## Close the loop with verification

The delivery team should reproduce the issue on a non-production environment where possible, record the root cause and define the smallest correction that addresses the problem. Test both the corrected path and related workflows that could regress. Verify the result at realistic viewport sizes, with keyboard navigation and applicable privacy choices. A green build alone is not proof that the visible issue is fixed. Communicate which version contains the change, any remaining limitation and how the visitor can confirm the result. For a support issue that cannot be reproduced, keep the report open for relevant evidence rather than asserting a fix. Record only necessary information and follow the approved retention schedule. This procedure is a proposed operational guide, not a promise of a specific response time, automatic ticket creation or live support availability.
